title: A Missed Opportunity: How the AFT Could Have Changed Teaching and Learning (and maybe still can)
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: After a ResearchEd conference in which speaker after speaker cited authors first popularized in the AFT's American Educator, Pondiscio asks why the union has not turned that legacy into influence. He credits the magazine with early coverage of Rosenshine, Willingham and E.D. Hirsch, and credits Al Shanker with championing Hirsch before reformers cared about curriculum. His complaint is not that unions look after their members but that the AFT, since Shanker, has failed to lead on curriculum and instruction. He argues that Randi Weingarten fills the flagship publication with partisan columns that do nothing for teachers hungry for cognitive science. Her stated reply is that the column is how leadership talks to members. Pondiscio concludes that the AFT could still act as something closer to a professional guild if it gave evidence-based practice attention and visibility.
points: American Educator was publishing Rosenshine, Willingham and Hirsch long before ResearchEd popularized them, so the union already holds the credibility the movement is seeking.
Pondiscio faults the AFT for failing to lead on classroom practice, not for protecting its members.
He argues partisan columns waste the magazine's platform when teachers want practical, evidence-based material.
Weingarten's reply, that the column is the union's channel to members, shows the editorial trade-off was deliberate.
The proposed move is for the AFT to behave like a guild that emphasizes professional development, knowledge-sharing and standards.
quotes: I lost track of the number of times I heard ResearchEd presenters name-drop Barak Rosenshine and his “Principles of Instruction,” which first appeared in the magazine’s Spring 2012 issue: ten steps, from reviewing prior learning to checking understanding, all grounded in cognitive science. ResearchEd speakers brandished it like a sword, slicing through “discovery learning” nonsense.

The greater sin of the AFT, at least in the decades since Al Shanker’s retirement, has been its failure to lead on curriculum and instruction—or even give it much oxygen at all. Worse, AFT President Randi Weingarten routinely takes to the pages of American Educator to unburden herself of predictable political rants, complaining about the Trump administration’s “chaos, confusion, corruption, and cronyism” in the current issue, for example.

Such partisan tub-thumping does little for teachers more eager to learn about cognitive load theory than how “the Biden-Harris administration guided the country to the strongest post-COVID economy in the world.

Teachers unions are a reliable bogeyman—cartoon villains guarding tenure and stagnation and indifferent to children. I’ve never been of the mind to criticize them for doing what unions were created to do. But I do fault the AFT for not leading on classroom practice in recent years.

Weingarten likes to remind people that she was a high school teacher but she rarely discusses classroom practice with any seriousness or sophistication. Her Twitter feed is a litany of hot takes on Ukraine, democracy, healthcare, Trump, etc. Effective teaching? Barely a whisper.

Fair enough, and it’s Weingarten’s prerogative to use her platform how she sees fit. But the AFT’s history of recognizing and publishing important thinkers in American Educator suggests its capacity to serve not just as a labor union but as something closer to a guild, with equal emphasis on professional development, knowledge-sharing, and maintaining standards within the profession.

So, two cheers for the old AFT and the American Educator. For those who’ve been paying attention, it’s long been a reliable source of first-rate research and practice tips for those who think teaching should run on evidence, not folklore and philosophy. It could still be an important engine of K-12 instructional reform still today.
